name: Chloe Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you tell me is confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a 240-tonne haul truck at an open-pit copper mine, and I lead a crew of eight on night shift. We start at six at night with the pre-start meeting, then I walk round my truck with a torch and a paper checklist. After that it's twelve hours of loading at the shovel, hauling up the ramp and tipping at the crusher, round and round. I'm hired through a labour-hire company, so I earn less than the company's own drivers sitting in the same seat.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the size of it. When you've got a full load on the ramp at three in the morning and the whole pit is lit up below you, there's nothing like it. What wears me out is the nights and the money. Jonah, my partner, works in the mine canteen, and between us we've got rent, a car loan and about two weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the trucks still need me, and the bosses still pay me less than they should. That sounds like a normal Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about the real problems. At the union meeting I'd bring up the labour-hire rates again, because that's what hurts people here. AI being hype doesn't fix the fact that I do the same job as the staff drivers for less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved, but not calm. My job's safe in that world, but my money isn't. One bad month, like the car needing a new gearbox, and we're borrowing from my partner Jonah's mum again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and push for the labour-hire drivers to get put on as staff, that's the fight. I'd sign up two more people from my crew to the union before Christmas. And we'd keep cutting back, so no takeaway on days off and no trip home for my sister's birthday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It's not fear, it's the grind of always being one bill away from trouble. Nothing in that picture changes that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would go unpaid first if a bad month came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car loan, probably, because the landlord won't wait and you can't skip food. But I need the car to get to the mine, it's forty minutes out on the highway. So really nothing can go unpaid, and that's the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lead a crew. Who on it would you worry about, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rhys, our youngest, he's twenty and sends half his pay to his mum. If the labour-hire firm loses the contract, he's gone first. I watch out for him on shift and I'd do the same off shift.

say: AI hype doesn't fix my **real problem**, which is labour-hire pay below the staff drivers.
I'd use union meetings to push for **equal rates**, not to talk about computers.
think: My **job is safe** in this world, but my money still isn't.
One broken **gearbox** would put us back to borrowing from family.
do: **Push** the labour-hire drivers to be taken on as staff through the union.
**Sign up** two more crew members to the union before Christmas.
Cut **takeaways** and skip the trip home for my sister's birthday.
feel: **Tired** from always being one bill away from trouble, more than scared.
S0.quote: My job's safe in that world, but my money isn't. One bad month, like the car needing a new gearbox, and we're borrowing from my partner Jonah's mum again.
fieldNote: She treats AI as a **distraction** from the pay gap between labour-hire and staff drivers.
With **two weeks** of savings and a forty-minute commute, any shock hits the household hard.
Her protectiveness of **Rhys** shows she sees herself as responsible for the crew.

steps.text: Bring the labour-hire pay gap to the next union meeting
Keep driving night shifts on the same truck
Stop takeaways on days off and skip the trip home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots spreading slowly. We've already heard the company's looking at driverless trucks. So slowly could mean my truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company owes us a plan before it parks a single driverless truck in this pit. At work I'd tell the crew to get to the union meeting, because this is when you need numbers. Online I'd share the stories from other mines where they automated and the town went quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the haul trucks are the first thing they'd automate, because it's already been done at other mines. I'm good at my job, but being the best driver doesn't count much against a truck that never needs a toilet break. And labour-hire people go first, everybody knows that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the union to demand that any automation comes with retraining and first offer of the new jobs to current drivers. I'd stop the car loan early if I could, sell the car and share Jonah's lift. I'm not going to go learn computers, though, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, like they're already planning it behind our backs. And a bit sick, because I don't know what else I'd do out here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn computers. If the new jobs were in the control room, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd probably lose out, I know that. I've never used one of those AI things and I don't want to start. I'd rather fight for the jobs we've got than go chasing ones I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonah the night you heard the first driverless trucks were coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not panicking yet, but we're not buying anything either. Then I'd probably go for a long walk round the town. There's one road out of here and I'd be thinking about where it goes.

say: The company owes drivers a **plan** before a single driverless truck arrives.
I'd tell the crew to come to **union meetings**, because numbers matter now.
think: **Haul trucks** are the first thing they'd automate, since other mines already have.
Being the **best driver** counts little, and labour-hire workers go first.
do: **Demand** retraining and first offer of new jobs for current drivers.
**Sell the car** and share Jonah's lift to clear the loan.
Refuse to **learn AI tools**, and fight for existing jobs instead.
feel: **Angry** that the company seems to be planning behind the drivers' backs.
**Sick** at the thought of having nothing else to do in town.
S1.quote: Being the best driver doesn't count much against a truck that never needs a toilet break. And labour-hire people go first, everybody knows that.
fieldNote: She sees haul trucks as the **front line** of automation and herself as exposed.
Her **refusal** to learn new tools sits uneasily beside her fear of losing her seat.
She turns to **collective action** first and money cuts second.

steps.text: Get the union to demand retraining before any driverless trucks
Sell the hatchback and share Jonah's lift to the mine
Hold onto the driving job and refuse control-room training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking stuff, five for the robots. That's not much for a town that's only got one mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need government to step in, with a proper income for people whose jobs get taken. At work I'd say the union has to be at the table now, not in 2031. Online I'd be the one posting about it every day, probably annoying everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My driving is hands-on, so I'd get roughly until 2031. But the dispatchers and planners go in 2028, and once the planning is done by a machine, driverless trucks are an easy next step. I'd be watching the office people lose their jobs and knowing I'm three years behind them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union to fight for a deal now: redundancy pay for labour-hire drivers, not just staff. I'd vote for whoever promises a basic income, and I'd help run the campaign in town. And Jonah and I would start talking about moving back to the city, to his family, before the rent there gets even worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. Three years sounds like time, but with two weeks of savings it's nothing. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said three years sounds like time. What would you do in those three years that you wouldn't otherwise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save every cent, which is a joke on my pay. Maybe I'd take every overtime shift going, even with my back. I wouldn't retrain for something that's also going to be a robot by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who own the mine and the tech companies selling them the trucks. They'll make more than ever and the town gets nothing. A machine doesn't shop at the bakery on the main street.

say: Government should give people who lose jobs a **proper income**.
The **union** has to be negotiating now, not when the trucks arrive in 2031.
think: My driving lasts until about **2031**, three years after the planners and dispatchers go.
Once **machines plan** the haul, driverless trucks become an easy next step.
do: **Fight** for redundancy pay that covers labour-hire drivers, not only staff.
**Campaign** in town for candidates who back a basic income.
Start planning a **move** to the city near Jonah's family.
feel: **Scared** and lying awake doing sums, because three years means little with two weeks saved.
S2.quote: A machine doesn't shop at the bakery on the main street.
fieldNote: She grasps the **three-year gap**: planners go first, then trucks follow.
She blames **owners and tech firms**, and wants government income support.
She'd take **overtime** despite her back, rather than retrain for something also at risk.

steps.text: Fight through the union for redundancy pay covering labour-hire drivers
Help run the basic income campaign in town
Plan a move to the city near Jonah's family

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots three years after. So 2034 for my truck. I'd be thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, we need a plan for whole towns, not just for companies. At work I'd keep pushing the union to get it in writing. I'd tell people not to wait for the company to be nice about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means the first couple go by and nothing much happens to me, and that's dangerous. People get comfortable. Then the office jobs go in 2031 and suddenly everyone's scared at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get the union to set up a fund, a few dollars a week from everyone, for when the cuts come. I'd pay off the car loan, which I could do in about two years if I'm careful. And I'd keep my head down and keep driving, because I'm still needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less panicky than the fast one, but heavy. Like knowing the pit's going to close but not when.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd never learn AI tools. With eight years until robots reach your truck, would you change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd learn enough not to get fooled by it. But I'm not going to retrain to be the person who watches screens of trucks I used to drive. That's not a job, that's a funeral.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Rhys, the young guy on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Rhys to go and get a trade that needs hands and judgement, like an electrician, while he's young. I'd tell him not to wait for me or the union to save him. He's got time, which I don't really have.

say: We need a **plan for towns**, not just for the companies.
Don't wait for the company to be **kind**; get it in writing.
think: The **slow start** is dangerous, because people get comfortable.
Then the **office jobs** go in 2031 and everyone panics together.
do: **Set up** a union hardship fund paid a few dollars a week.
**Pay off** the car loan within about two years.
**Keep driving**, because the truck still needs her until about 2034.
feel: **Heavy**, like knowing the pit will close without knowing when.
S3.quote: I'm not going to retrain to be the person who watches screens of trucks I used to drive. That's not a job, that's a funeral.
fieldNote: Five years makes her **less frantic** but still sure she loses her seat.
Her advice to **Rhys** shows she sees more hope for others than for herself.
Her plan centres on a **hardship fund**, a collective answer, not a personal one.

steps.text: Set up a union hardship fund of a few dollars a week
Pay off the car loan within two years
Keep driving night shifts while the truck still needs her

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years for the thinking stuff and thirteen for robots. I'd be forty. That's a different conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse if governments and companies don't. At work I'd push for retraining money to be built into the next pay deal. Online I'd probably be quieter, because people tune out when it's that far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think I might get most of my working life in a truck after all, or close to it. That's a relief. But my money doesn't get better just because the robots are slower, I'd still be on labour-hire pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep pushing for staff positions, that's still the main fight. I'd try to build up three months of savings over a few years. And maybe, in a few years, I'd look at a heavy vehicle licence so I could drive road trains if the mine goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. It's like a storm forecast for next year, you still check the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A road train licence is a change from what you said earlier. What makes it feel different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still driving, still hands and eyes and judgement. It's not sitting at a screen. If I've got years to do it, I can do it without feeling like I've given in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Jonah plan differently with that much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably stay in town longer and maybe even think about kids in a few years. Jonah wants them more than me. With two years' warning we wouldn't dream of it.

say: Ten years is **enough time**, so governments and companies have no excuse.
The next pay deal should include **retraining money**.
think: I might get most of my **working life** in a truck after all.
Slower robots don't fix my **labour-hire pay**.
do: Keep pushing for **staff positions** for labour-hire drivers.
Build up **three months** of savings over a few years.
Look into a **road train licence** in a few years.
feel: **Calmer**, but still checking the roof for a storm forecast next year.
S4.quote: My money doesn't get better just because the robots are slower, I'd still be on labour-hire pay.
fieldNote: A decade lets her consider **retraining** only when it stays hands-on driving.
Her **money pressure** stays the same whatever the AI timeline.
Time opens up **family plans** she would not consider in the fast picture.

steps.text: Push for labour-hire drivers to become staff in the next deal
Put aside enough each payday to reach three months saved
Get a road train licence as a backup in a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. Three years between the office going and my truck going, with two weeks of savings, in a town with one mine. What would help is the union getting labour-hire drivers the same deal as staff, and a government income for towns like ours while people work out what's next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. Everyone talks about jobs, but if the mine runs itself, the school, the pub and the clinic close too. I'd want someone to ask what happens to the places, not just the people.

headlineQuote: If the mine runs itself, the school, the pub and the clinic close too.
portrait: Chloe is a **27-year-old** haul truck driver who leads a night crew at an open-pit copper mine.
She is on **labour-hire pay** below staff drivers and has about two weeks of savings.
She is a **union** voice who never uses AI and refuses control-room retraining.
She moves from **anxious** in AI Plateau to alarmed when AGI comes in 2028 or 2031.
With **ten years** she would consider a road train licence and even having kids.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, with three years between office jobs and her truck going.
whatWouldHelp: The **union** winning labour-hire drivers the same deal as staff.
A **government income** for one-mine towns while people work out their next step.
